Each concept is explained step-by-step with interactive code examples from @PoeticGlenn. 📖 Introduction Before you can build web apps, analyze data, or automate tasks, you need a rock-solid grasp of Python's fundamentals. This curriculum, designed by @PoeticGlenn, takes you from zero to confident in writing clean, efficient Python code. We'll cover variables, data types, control flow, functions, and essential data structures — everything you need to start building real projects. Learn the core concepts that apply to any programming language, not just Python syntax. From simple scripts to small applications, you'll have the skills to build what you imagine. Mastering basics ensures you can learn advanced topics like OOP, data science, and web development. "Everyone should learn to program a computer, because it teaches you how to think." — Steve Jobs 🐍 🚀 Why Learn This Curriculum Python's simplicity and readability make it the perfect first language, but its power makes it a career-long companion. This curriculum, curated by @PoeticGlenn, focuses on the 20% of Python that you'll use 80% of the time, giving you a strong foundation for any path you choose. Variables, loops, and conditionals are the same in every language. Learn them once, use them everywhere. Python's lists, dictionaries, and strings are incredibly powerful. Master them to manipulate data effectively. Learn to write reusable functions and modules so you can build and share your own toolkits. Whether you want to be a web developer, data scientist, or DevOps engineer, basics are your first step. @PoeticGlenn says: "Don't rush the basics. The time you invest now will pay off tenfold in every project you build." 🌍 Significance in the Programming World Python is the language of choice for web development, data science, AI, automation, and more. Understanding its fundamentals opens doors to countless opportunities. This curriculum, designed by @PoeticGlenn, reflects the core knowledge required to contribute to Python projects anywhere. Build backends with Django, Flask, or FastAPI. Python powers the web. Pandas, NumPy, TensorFlow, and PyTorch — the AI revolution runs on Python. Script repetitive tasks, manage infrastructure, and build CI/CD pipelines. The fundamentals you're about to learn are the same building blocks used by Google, NASA, and Spotify. Jump to any section — all entries are equal size 📖 Introduction 🚀 Why Learn This 🌍 Significance 🏷️ Variables & Assignment 🗂️ Data Types 🔀 Conditionals 🔄 Loops 📦 Functions 📋 Lists 📖 Dictionaries 📝 Strings ❓ FAQ 💛 Outro Variables are names that point to values. They are the building blocks of any program. Use = to assign a value to a variable. No declaration needed — Python infers the type. Step 1: Assign the integer 25 to the variable age. Step 2: Assign the string "Alice" to the variable name. Step 3: Assign the float 3.14 to the variable pi. Step 4: Assign the boolean True to the variable is_student. Step 5: Use the type() function to show the data type of each variable. Step 6: Print the values using f-strings. python Copy Run age = 25 name = "Alice" pi = 3.14 is_student = True print(f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}") print(f"pi = {pi}, Type of pi: {type(pi)}") print(f"Student: {is_student}") 💡 Python is dynamically typed — you don't need to specify the type when declaring a variable. Variables can be reassigned to new values at any time. Step 1: Assign score = 10 and print it. Step 2: Reassign score = 20 and print it. Step 3: Reassign score = "high" (changing type) and print it. Step 4: Use type() to show that the type changed from int to str. python Copy Run score = 10 print(f"Score: {score}, Type: {type(score)}") score = 20 print(f"Score: {score}, Type: {type(score)}") score = "high" print(f"Score: {score}, Type: {type(score)}") Assign multiple variables in one line — useful for swapping values. Step 1: Assign a, b, c = 1, 2, 3 and print them. Step 2: Swap a and b using a, b = b, a. Step 3: Print the new values to verify the swap. python Copy Run a, b, c = 1, 2, 3 print(f"a={a}, b={b}, c={c}") a, b = b, a print(f"After swap: a={a}, b={b}") Understanding data types is crucial for writing correct programs. Integers are whole numbers. Floats are numbers with decimals. Step 1: Create an integer x = 5 and a float y = 3.14. Step 2: Perform basic arithmetic: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division. Step 3: Use type() to show the type of each result. Step 4: Show integer division // and exponentiation **. python Copy Run x = 5 y = 3.14 print(f"x = {x} (type: {type(x)})") print(f"y = {y} (type: {type(y)})") print(f"x + y = {x + y}") print(f"x * y = {x * y}") print(f"x / y = {x / y}") print(f"x // 2 = {x // 2}") Strings are sequences of characters. Use single or double quotes. Step 1: Create a string name = "Alice". Step 2: Use f-strings for interpolation: f"Hello, {name}". Step 3: Concatenate strings with +: "Hello, " + name. Step 4: Show string multiplication: "ha" * 3. Step 5: Use len() to get the string length. python Copy Run name = "Alice" greeting = f"Hello, {name}" print(greeting) print("Concatenation: " + name) print("ha" * 3) print(f"Length of name: {len(name)}") Booleans represent True or False. They are the result of comparisons. Step 1: Create booleans is_raining = False and has_umbrella = True. Step 2: Use logical operators and, or, not. Step 3: Show comparisons: 5 > 3, 5 == 5, 5 != 3. python Copy Run is_raining = False has_umbrella = True print(f"Is raining: {is_raining}") print(f"Has umbrella: {has_umbrella}") print(f"Raining AND has umbrella: {is_raining and has_umbrella}") print(f"Raining OR has umbrella: {is_raining or has_umbrella}") print(f"NOT raining: {not is_raining}") print(f"5 > 3: {5 > 3}") print(f"5 == 5: {5 == 5}") Make decisions in your code based on conditions. The simplest form of conditional. Step 1: Assign age = 18. Step 2: Write an if statement: if age >= 18:. Step 3: Indent the block to execute when the condition is True. Step 4: The block runs if the condition is True. python Copy Run age = 18 if age >= 18: print("You are an adult.") print("You can vote.") Handle both True and False cases. Step 1: Assign temperature = 25. Step 2: Check if temperature > 30:. Step 3: If True, print "It's hot outside.". Step 4: In the else block, print "It's not too hot.". python Copy Run temperature = 25 if temperature > 30: print("It's hot outside.") else: print("It's not too hot.") Chain multiple conditions with elif. Step 1: Assign score = 85. Step 2: Check multiple ranges using elif. Step 3: Print the corresponding grade. python Copy Run score = 85 if score >= 90: print("Grade: A") elif score >= 80: print("Grade: B") elif score >= 70: print("Grade: C") elif score >= 60: print("Grade: D") else: print("Grade: F") Repeat code blocks efficiently. Use for to iterate over lists, strings, ranges, etc. Step 1: Create a list of colors: colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]. Step 2: Write a for loop: for color in colors:. Step 3: Print each color. Step 4: Use range() to iterate over numbers. python Copy Run colors = ["red", "green", "blue"] for color in colors: print(f"Color: {color}") print("\nNumbers 1 to 3:") for i in range(1, 4): print(f"Number: {i}") Use while when you don't know how many times to iterate. Step 1: Initialize count = 0. Step 2: Write while count < 5:. Step 3: Print the count and increment it. Step 4: The loop stops when count >= 5. python Copy Run count = 0 while count < 5: print(f"Count: {count}") count += 1 print("Loop finished!") ⚠️ Be careful with while loops — if the condition never becomes False, you create an infinite loop. Functions let you organize, reuse, and structure your code. Use def to define a function. Step 1: Define greet() using def. Step 2: The function body is indented. Step 3: Call the function using greet(). Step 4: Define a function with a parameter. python Copy Run def greet(): print("Hello, world!") greet() def greet_person(name): print(f"Hello, {name}!") greet_person("Alice") Use return to send a value back to the caller. Step 1: Define add(a, b) that returns a + b. Step 2: Call the function and store the result in result. Step 3: Print the result. python Copy Run def add(a, b): return a + b result = add(5, 3) print(f"Result: {result}") Provide default values for parameters. Step 1: Define greet(name, greeting="Hello"). Step 2: Call with just the name: greet("Alice"). Step 3: Call with a custom greeting: greet("Bob", "Hi"). python Copy Run def greet(name, greeting="Hello"): print(f"{greeting}, {name}!") greet("Alice") greet("Bob", "Hi") Lists are one of the most versatile data structures in Python. Access elements by index (starting from 0). Step 1: Create a list: fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]. Step 2: Access the first element: fruits[0]. Step 3: Access the last element with negative index: fruits[-1]. Step 4: Use slicing: fruits[1:3]. python Copy Run fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] print(f"First fruit: {fruits[0]}") print(f"Last fruit: {fruits[-1]}") print(f"Slicing 1 to 3: {fruits[1:3]}") Lists are mutable — you can change them in place. Step 1: Create an empty list: items = []. Step 2: Add an item using append(). Step 3: Insert an item at a specific position using insert(). Step 4: Remove an item using remove(). python Copy Run items = [] items.append("first") items.append("second") print(f"After append: {items}") items.insert(0, "zero") print(f"After insert: {items}") items.remove("second") print(f"After remove: {items}") Combine lists and loops for powerful data processing. Step 1: Create a list of numbers: numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Step 2: Use a for loop to calculate the sum. Step 3: Use enumerate() to get both index and value. python Copy Run numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] total = 0 for num in numbers: total += num print(f"Sum: {total}") for i, num in enumerate(numbers): print(f"Index {i}: {num}") Dictionaries store data in key-value pairs, making data retrieval fast and intuitive. Use curly braces {} and colons : to separate keys and values. Step 1: Create a dictionary: person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}. Step 2: Access a value using square brackets: person["name"]. Step 3: Use get() to avoid KeyError: person.get("city"). Step 4: Add a new key-value pair: person["city"] = "New York". python Copy Run person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30} print(f"Name: {person['name']}") print(f"Age: {person['age']}") print(f"City (using get): {person.get('city', 'unknown')}") person["city"] = "New York" print(f"City after adding: {person['city']}") Iterate over keys, values, or both. Step 1: Create a dictionary: grades = {"Alice": 90, "Bob": 85}. Step 2: Loop over keys using for key in grades:. Step 3: Loop over values using for value in grades.values():. Step 4: Loop over items using for key, value in grades.items():. python Copy Run grades = {"Alice": 90, "Bob": 85, "Charlie": 92} print("Keys:") for key in grades: print(f" {key}") print("Values:") for value in grades.values(): print(f" {value}") print("Items:") for name, score in grades.items(): print(f" {name}: {score}") Python strings come with a rich set of methods for text processing. Use methods like .upper(), .lower(), .strip(), and .replace(). Step 1: Create a string: text = " Hello, Python! ". Step 2: Remove whitespace with .strip(). Step 3: Convert to uppercase and lowercase. Step 4: Replace substrings with .replace(). Step 5: Split a string into a list with .split(). python Copy Run text = " Hello, Python! " print(f"Original: '{text}'") stripped = text.strip() print(f"Stripped: '{stripped}'") print(f"Uppercase: {stripped.upper()}") print(f"Lowercase: {stripped.lower()}") replaced = stripped.replace("Python", "World") print(f"Replaced: {replaced}") words = stripped.split(", ") print(f"Split: {words}") Use f-strings or .format() to embed variables in strings. Step 1: Define variables: name = "Alice", age = 30. Step 2: Use an f-string to embed variables: f"My name is {name}.". Step 3: Use .format() for older codebases. python Copy Run name = "Alice" age = 30 print(f"My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.") print("My name is {} and I am {} years old.".format(name, age)) Common questions about Python fundamentals, answered. + Python is dynamically typed. You don't need to declare the type of a variable; Python infers it at runtime. You can reassign a variable to a value of a different type. + Lists are mutable (you can change them), while tuples are immutable (cannot be changed after creation). Tuples are faster and use less memory, and they can be used as dictionary keys. + Indentation is Python's way of defining blocks of code. Unlike languages that use braces, Python uses indentation to group statements. This enforces readability and reduces syntax clutter. + It ensures that a block of code runs only if the script is executed directly, not when imported as a module. It's a standard pattern for making Python files both reusable modules and executable scripts. + Use built-in functions: int(), float(), str(), list(), tuple(), dict(). For example, int("10") gives the integer 10, and str(10) gives the string "10". + == checks if the values are equal, while is checks if they refer to the same object in memory. Use == for value comparison, and is for identity comparison (e.g., None). + Use print() statements to inspect variables. For more advanced debugging, use the built-in pdb module (import pdb; pdb.set_trace()). Many IDEs also offer graphical debugging tools. Congratulations!
